title: Context Engineering for Reliable Agent Workflows
summary: This intermediate-level module teaches you to assemble, order, inspect, and revise the information supplied to an agent workflow. After completing it, you can diagnose context-related failures and design a context pipeline that keeps instructions, retrieved evidence, working state, and observations distinguishable.
objectives: Construct a context pipeline that selects and organizes instructions, evidence, working state, and observations.
Diagnose whether a workflow failure came from missing, irrelevant, poorly positioned, or stale context.
Choose when to retrieve source material instead of placing all potentially useful material into every request.
Preserve enough provenance to trace an output back to the context that supported it.

sections.title: What changed in this update
paragraphs: The previous citation was the repository path content/modules/reliable-agent-workflows/context-engineering.json. It had an unregistered publisher and had never been verified, and it was not a directly accessible HTTPS research source.

This update replaces that citation record with canonical HTTPS records for research on retrieval-augmented generation, the use of information within long contexts, and workflows that interleave reasoning with actions. The change affects source provenance, verification dates, and the evidence supporting the guidance about retrieval, context position, and action observations. The module remains provider-neutral and introduces no named tool, version, or configuration key.

sections.title: A working definition of context engineering
paragraphs: In this module, context engineering means deliberately selecting, organizing, and maintaining the information available to a model during a workflow. Context can include task instructions, retrieved source passages, user input, intermediate state, action observations, and prior messages.

An agent workflow is a process in which model outputs can guide later operations and the resulting observations can become input to another model step. Research on interleaving reasoning and actions provides an example of this structure. Reliable context engineering therefore covers both the initial input and the information carried forward after each operation.

This is an intermediate-level module. It assumes basic familiarity with prompts, model inputs and outputs, and multi-step workflows. It does not assume knowledge of a particular provider, product, programming language, or context limit.

sections.title: Build a context pipeline
paragraphs: Begin by identifying the information required for the current decision. Separate binding task instructions from supporting evidence, current working state, and observations produced by earlier operations. This separation makes it easier to detect conflicts and to determine why a later output used a particular fact.

Select context according to the current step rather than carrying every available item into every request. Retrieval-augmented generation research shows a pattern in which relevant external passages are retrieved and supplied for generation. For workflow design, the practical lesson is to retrieve evidence when it becomes relevant and retain its source identity.

Order the selected material deliberately. Research on long contexts found that performance can depend on where relevant information appears, with information in the middle sometimes used less effectively than information near the beginning or end. Do not assume that inclusion alone guarantees use. Place critical instructions and directly relevant evidence where their roles are explicit, and test the ordering with representative tasks.

After an operation, add its observation to the working state only if a later step needs it. Record what produced the observation and distinguish it from instructions. Before the next request, remove stale or duplicated material while preserving facts that remain necessary.
sections.callout: More context is not automatically better context. Relevance, role, position, freshness, and provenance all affect whether the supplied information is useful.

sections.title: Diagnose context failures
paragraphs: When a workflow produces an unsupported or incorrect result, inspect the context actually supplied at the failing step. First ask whether required information was absent. If it was present, ask whether irrelevant material competed with it, whether its role was unclear, whether it was poorly positioned, or whether a stale observation contradicted newer evidence.

Classify the failure before changing the workflow. A missing-context failure calls for retrieval or state preservation. An irrelevant-context failure calls for stricter selection. A position or role failure calls for reordering or clearer separation. A stale-context failure calls for replacement or explicit invalidation.

Keep a trace that connects each step with its instructions, selected evidence, incoming state, operation observations, and resulting output. The trace lets you compare the context the workflow was intended to use with the context it actually received. Avoid recording sensitive material unless the workflow is authorized to retain it.

sections.title: Apply a repeatable review procedure
paragraphs: For each workflow step, state the decision the model must make. List the minimum instructions, evidence, state, and observations required for that decision. Remove unrelated items, label the role of each remaining item in plain language, and arrange the material so that critical information is easy to distinguish.

Run representative cases and inspect both the output and the supplied context. Include a case with missing evidence, a case with distracting evidence, and a case with an updated observation. A successful review confirms that the workflow retrieves missing support, excludes distractions, and replaces stale state.

After this module, you can do more than write a single prompt. You can design and inspect the information flow across a multi-step agent workflow, identify the class of a context failure, and choose a targeted correction instead of adding material indiscriminately.

questions.prompt: What did the source correction in this update affect?
choices: It introduced a required named tool and version.
It changed source provenance, verification dates, and the evidence supporting guidance about retrieval, context position, and action observations.
It established a universal context limit.
It changed the module from intermediate to advanced.
questions.explanation: The source-correction section states that the replacement affects provenance, verification dates, and the evidence for retrieval, position, and action-observation guidance.

questions.prompt: When does the module recommend retrieving source material?
choices: When it becomes relevant to the current step.
Only after the workflow has produced its final output.
Whenever all available material can be copied into every request.
Only when no task instructions exist.
questions.explanation: The context-pipeline section recommends selecting context for the current step and retrieving external evidence when it becomes relevant.

questions.prompt: Why should a designer test the position of important information?
choices: Because information can be used differently depending on where it appears in a long context.
Because every important passage must appear only in the middle.
Because ordering matters only for action observations.
Because including information guarantees that the model will use it.
questions.explanation: The module cites research finding that performance can depend on the position of relevant information and warns that inclusion alone does not guarantee use.

questions.prompt: What is the targeted response to a stale-context failure?
choices: Replace or explicitly invalidate the stale information.
Repeat the same context without inspection.
questions.explanation: The failure-diagnosis section says that stale context should be replaced or explicitly invalidated.
